source.title: Words That Make Language Models Perceive
source.authors: Sophie L. Wang; Phillip Isola; Brian Cheung

record.tranche_reason: Uses mutual-kNN alignment, the measure associated with the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, to test alignment across model scales and paired sensory data; it adds generative representations and sensory-prompt conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Huh et al.'s prior convergence result but those cited results are not recorded as this study's rows. VQA accuracy and DreamSim image-generation results are downstream task outcomes, not measurements of representational alignment, so they are not rows. Appendix C reports additional encoder, dataset, and language-model results; selected textual findings about encoder supervision are recorded below, but the plotted breakdowns are not transcribed into separate rows.
record.test_reason: Uses the Platonic Representation Hypothesis recipe: mutual-kNN alignment between frozen text-only LLMs (Qwen3 0.6B–32B) and frozen vision/audio encoders on paired caption data, including WiT as in Huh et al. It reports how alignment changes with LLM scale, representation extraction, prompt cues, input content and encoder supervision. It is not one of the original sources, though two authors overlap with the PRH paper.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that sensory prompting ('see'/'hear') steers generative representations of text-only LLMs toward vision or audio encoder geometry. They report that alignment grows with generation length and model size, and that modality separation sharpens with scale. They argue prior single-pass evaluations underestimate cross-modal alignment. They read the results as LLMs implicitly encoding latent sensory causes of text, extending passive convergence to inference-time steering. Language-supervised encoders align most.
record.recipe_differences: Uses mutual-kNN alignment to compare kernels as in the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, but applies it to generated LLM representations, sensory cues, and fixed specialist encoders rather than only single-pass representations.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment varies with generative versus single-pass representation, cue modality, prompt wording and instruction form, sensory-language ablation, generation length (including a decline at 512 tokens), layer, dataset, encoder supervision, and model size. Different instruction verbs also give slightly different alignment; the paper reports that “describe” can outperform “imagine.”

fits_no_version.finding: SEE–HEAR separability of the LLM's own embeddings grows with Qwen3 size (Table 2). Cohen's d rises 1.95→2.65 on WiT and 3.14→4.52 on AudioCaps; AUROC rises 0.92→0.97 and 0.98→1.00.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Modality-specific prompt-conditioned representations within an LLM become more separable with scale.

fits_no_version.finding: No-cue generations are closer to SEE than to HEAR generations (CKA and mutual-kNN), a visual default bias that diminishes with scale (Appendix D, Figures 26–28).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Text-only LLMs default to a visual framing absent explicit sensory cues.

fits_no_version.finding: SEE cue improves text-only VQA on MME (64.78→67.14, n=2334). SEE-cued sentences also give lower DreamSim distance in SDXL reconstructions (Table 1; Appendix H).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sensory prompting improves downstream perceptual tasks performed through text.

record.problems: The main alignment values are mostly presented in figures without exact numerical values in the text. The sensory encoders are fixed while language-model size changes, so the results do not test both sides improving together. The study notes possible hallucination of perceptual details and lower alignment to audio encoders.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted to meet the row limit. Appendix C's additional per-encoder, per-dataset, and per-language-model plotted results are not separately transcribed; the aggregate textual supervision comparisons are recorded in r34-r38.

untested.parts: Only the LLM side scales, within one family (Qwen3); the sensory encoders are fixed. The scale trend is stated only for matched sensory cues with 128-token generative representations. No stated scale trend for no-cue or single-pass embeddings. Other families (Llama, Phi-4) are not reported as a scale test.
Vision encoder capability is not varied, so 'both models get better' is untested. The scaling claim rests on figure-only values.
The similarity metric and k are not varied for LLM–encoder alignment. Out-of-distribution inputs are not tested.
No plateau with scale is tested. No direct test of shared data versus a common model of reality beyond the encoder-supervision contrast.

missing.what: Scale trend of alignment under single-pass (ze) and no-cue generative (zg) representations across Qwen3 0.6B–32B; plotted but not recorded as scaling rows
Absolute alignment levels stay low (mutual-kNN roughly 0.06–0.2 on figure axes, k=10), bearing on how far convergence is from complete

Further choice dependence: instruction form gives much higher alignment than non-instruction form; 'describe' beats 'imagine'; verbs differ slightly; alignment rises with generation length but can decline at 512 tokens; mean-layer embedding often beats any single layer
Alignment results for other LLM families (Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.2 1B/3B, Phi-4), including a small within-family size comparison for Llama 3.2
Per-encoder results for ViT-MAE, ViT-MSN, Audio-MAE, EAT and the DCI/Clotho datasets

record.verdict_notes: Authors include Isola and Cheung of the PRH paper, but this paper is not an original source. Most alignment values are figure-only, so scale and cue verdicts rest on the authors' statements. The study's main manipulation is prompting, which shows alignment is not a fixed property of a model; this is relevant to V6. The V7 support is indirect: the authors attribute CLIP/CLAP advantages to paired training but do not frame it against the common-reality explanation.

versions.untested_parts: Does not scale multiple independently trained sensory models alongside the language models, or vary their architectures, objectives, or training data systematically.
Tests increasing language-model size against fixed vision and audio encoders; it does not test whether both sides improve together.
Different initialization seeds and shared features or subspaces are not tested.
Mapping, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired interchangeability are not tested.
Recurring interpretable features or circuits are not tested.
The paper varies input wording and prompting, but does not compare different similarity metrics for language-to-sensory-encoder alignment or vary k for that alignment.
Does not establish a plateau or directly compare shared training data against a common underlying model of reality.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Single-pass embeddings and mismatched sensory cues
reader_labels.reason: Cue-related gains do not carry over to single-pass embeddings, and a mismatched cue lowers alignment to the other modality (r25, r28-r30).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Changing or replacing scene-appropriate sensory wording
reader_labels.reason: Ablating sensory language lowers alignment, while adding generic visual words fails to raise it and replacing captions with them lowers alignment further (r31-r33).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Encoders with language or semantic supervision compared with self-supervised encoders
reader_labels.reason: Language-supervised CLIP and CLAP align most strongly, self-supervised DINOv2 and BEATs align less strongly, and label fine-tuning raises BEATs alignment (r34-r38).
